source.title: The 10 Biggest Unsolved Problems in Physics

accepted.question_text: How can a single logically consistent physical theory make gravity and quantum physics coexist when general relativity and quantum mechanics already apply in overlapping domains but do not fit together, and when direct experimental tests of quantum-gravity effects appear far beyond present technology?

evidence.quote: The biggest unsolved problem in fundamental physics is how gravity and the quantum will be made to coexist within the same theory.
The problem is that quantum physics and general relativity already overlap each other’s domains, but do not fit together.

accepted.question_text: Why do the elementary particles have the particular masses they do, why can the many free parameters of the standard model not be calculated or predicted theoretically, and why do heavier second- and third-generation copies of first-generation matter particles exist at all if ordinary matter is built only from the first generation?

evidence.quote: These parameters cannot be calculated or predicted theoretically.
From a theoretical point of view, then, the particle masses are a total mystery - they might as well have been random numbers drawn from a hat.
What are the heavier ones for?

accepted.question_text: How and why does quantum measurement produce a single definite outcome from a wave function that allows many coexisting possibilities, and how does the definite macroscopic reality we observe emerge from microscopic quantum dynamics if quantum mechanics is supposed to apply universally at all scales?

evidence.quote: But how and why does a measurement on a particle make its wave function collapse, which in turn produces the concrete reality we perceive?
Why then do we not see ghostly superpositions of objects even at our level? This problem is still unsolved.

accepted.question_text: Can the behavior of turbulent fluids be understood in a general way, including whether the incompressible Navier-Stokes equations always have solutions and whether those solutions remain well behaved rather than developing singularities, or is turbulence fundamentally resistant to human mathematical and physical understanding?

evidence.quote: Turbulence has been called the last unsolved problem of classical physics.

it is not known whether a general solution to the Navier-Stokes equations (for incompressible fluids) even exists, and, if there is a solution, whether it fully describes the fluid or contains unknowable points - singularities.
Does turbulence exceed the human physical understanding and mathematical ability, or would it become intelligible if only we tackled it with the right methods?

accepted.question_text: What is the physical origin of the apparent accelerated expansion of the universe: does a real dark-energy component exist, and if so what is it, or is the acceleration only an effect of how cosmological data are interpreted?

evidence.quote: The surprise was therefore total when the observational data instead seemed to indicate that the universe is accelerating, i.e. increases its rate of expansion - as if the cosmos recently moved its foot from the brake pedal to the accelerator.
The mystery is that no one still knows what dark energy is (or if it even exists).

accepted.question_text: What is the unseen matter inferred from gravitational effects on visible matter, radiation, and cosmic structure formation, and does such dark matter actually exist as a new form of matter even though it neither emits nor absorbs light and has not been directly detected?

evidence.quote: Other observations indicate that about 90 percent of the matter itself in the universe is made up of an exotic, unknown variety that neither absorbs nor emits light.
the existence of dark matter is still hypothetical [8] and its large abundance derived from its gravitational effects on visible matter, radiation and structure formation in the universe.

accepted.question_text: Is the difficulty of predicting the behavior of even mildly complex systems from the four known fundamental forces merely a limitation of current theories and methods, or does nature require additional organizing principles beyond a small set of fundamental laws in order to account for emergent structure, life, and consciousness?

evidence.quote: it is almost always impossible to directly from them in detail predict the behavior of even mildly complex systems.
Is this a real aspect of nature, or just a result of our theories so far being formulated in non-ideal ways?

The logical possibility also exist that the world is not reductionist (or rather, constructionist), that is, that a handful of fundamental laws are not sufficient to build up (reconstruct) all the complexity that we see around us, but rather that these may have to be supplemented by new (unknown) principles on different scales.

accepted.question_text: Why did the early universe leave behind a small excess of matter instead of producing equal amounts of matter and antimatter that would have annihilated completely, given that the known CP violation is too weak to explain the observed matter-dominated universe?

evidence.quote: The question of why there is so much more matter than its oppositely charged mirror image, antimatter, is actually the crucial question of why anything exists at all [10].
This has not yet any explanation.
The problem is that the known CP-violation is far too weak and insignificant to explain why we today have only matter.

accepted.question_text: How does macroscopic friction arise in a world whose microscopic quantum description is frictionless, and what is the connection between friction, irreversible heat loss, structure formation, and the apparent one-way direction of time?

evidence.quote: in physics we still do not understand how something so “obvious” as friction arises.
But at the microscopic atomic level there is no friction
Everything, however, consists of atoms, so how can friction then appear on our level?

accepted.question_text: Why does time appear to have a preferred forward direction, why was the entropy of the universe so low in the past despite the early universe containing enormous energy in a very small region, and is time as represented in current physical theories perhaps not fundamental at all?

evidence.quote: the underlying and unresolved question then becomes: why was the entropy so low in the past?
this symmetry breaking is far too weak to explain the time arrow
Maybe even time, as we so far have described it in our theories, is really just an illusion [13]?
